q: Which HIV envelope protein pulls the viral envelope into the host cell membrane during fusion?
x: After gp120 binds CD4 and a coreceptor, gp41, the other half of the env protein, folds back and pulls the viral envelope against the host membrane so the two fuse. Enfuvirtide binds gp41 and blocks this step, so it is a fusion inhibitor.

w.gp120: gp120 is the surface subunit that docks onto CD4 and then onto CCR5 or CXCR4. It mediates attachment, not the fusion that follows.
w.p24: p24 is the capsid protein of the core inside the virion and the antigen picked up early by fourth-generation tests. It lies within the envelope and plays no part in fusion.
w.p17 matrix protein: p17 is the matrix protein lining the inner face of the envelope. It helps assemble virions and does not drive fusion.
w.Integrase: Integrase is a pol enzyme that inserts viral DNA into the host chromosome. It acts inside the cell long after fusion.

pt.say: In step 2, Fusion, gp41 pulls the envelope into the cell membrane, and enfuvirtide binds gp41 to block it.

q: Which test is required before prescribing maraviroc to a patient with HIV?
x: Maraviroc blocks CCR5 on the host cell, so it works only against strains that use CCR5. A tropism assay checks whether the patient's virus uses CCR5, CXCR4 or both, because CXCR4-using virus, more common late in disease, would escape the drug.

w.HLA-B*57:01 genotype: HLA-B*57:01 testing predicts abacavir hypersensitivity. It belongs to the NRTI abacavir, not to maraviroc.
w.Hepatitis B serology: Hepatitis B status is checked before any antiretroviral regimen, because stopping tenofovir or lamivudine can flare hepatitis B. It does not decide whether to use maraviroc.
w.G6PD enzyme activity: G6PD testing comes before drugs that can cause oxidative hemolysis, such as dapsone and primaquine. Maraviroc does not cause hemolysis.
w.Baseline CD4 count: The CD4 count stages immune damage and guides prophylaxis against opportunistic infections. It does not tell which coreceptor the virus uses.

pt.say: Step 1 shows maraviroc blocking CCR5 beside the label that the coreceptor is CCR5 or CXCR4, so a coreceptor tropism assay must show which one the patient's virus uses.

q: Which coreceptor is used by the HIV strains that emerge late in disease and predict faster CD4 decline?
x: Early infection is dominated by CCR5-using, macrophage-tropic virus. Over years, strains that use CXCR4 on T cells emerge in many patients and are linked with faster CD4 decline. This switch also explains why maraviroc needs a tropism test.

w.CCR5: CCR5 on macrophages and memory T cells is the coreceptor of the strains that dominate early infection and are usually transmitted.
w.CD4 receptor: CD4 is the primary receptor for every HIV strain at every stage. gp120 binds it first, so it cannot be what separates the late strains.
w.CD8: CD8 marks cytotoxic T cells, which attack infected cells. HIV entry needs CD4 and a chemokine receptor, never CD8.
w.CCR7: CCR7 directs naive T cells and dendritic cells toward lymph nodes. It is not an HIV coreceptor in practice; the two that matter are CCR5 and CXCR4.

pt.say: Step 1 states that gp120 binds CD4 and then a coreceptor, CCR5 or CXCR4; the CXCR4-using strains are the T-cell-tropic ones that emerge late.

q: Which feature of HIV replication selects drug-resistant mutants so quickly?
x: Reverse transcriptase has no proofreading function, so it makes frequent copying errors, and billions of virions are made each day. A mutation that blunts one drug is selected quickly under single-drug pressure, which is why therapy always combines drugs.

w.Reassortment of segmented genome pieces: Reassortment swaps whole segments between viruses in one cell, as in influenza. HIV has a single unsegmented RNA genome, so its variation comes mainly from copying errors.
w.Latency in resting CD4 cells: Latent provirus in resting CD4 cells explains why viral load rebounds when therapy stops. A silent genome is not copying itself, so it does not make new resistant mutants.
w.Random integration into host chromosomes: Integration makes infection permanent, but where the DNA lands does not change the drug targets. Mutations arise while RNA is copied into DNA.
w.Antigenic shift of envelope genes: Antigenic shift is the reassortment-driven change in influenza hemagglutinin and neuraminidase. HIV varies by point mutation during copying, not by shift.

hl: Three drugs are combined because error-prone copying selects resistance to any one.
pt.say: Step 3 notes that RNA is copied into DNA with frequent errors, and the bottom line says error-prone copying selects resistance, so reverse transcription without proofreading is the cause.

q: Which antiretroviral class blocks insertion of viral DNA into the host chromosome?
x: Integrase strand transfer inhibitors, the -tegravir drugs such as dolutegravir, block the step where integrase inserts the DNA copy of the viral genome into a host chromosome. The provirus is then never made.

w.Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibit: NRTIs act one step earlier. They end the growing DNA chain during reverse transcription, so they stop DNA from being made rather than stop its insertion.
w.Nonnucleoside reverse transcriptase inhi: NNRTIs such as efavirenz bind reverse transcriptase at an allosteric site, so they also act before integration. They never touch the integrase enzyme.
w.Protease inhibitors: Protease inhibitors act late, after budding, by blocking cleavage of gag-pol polyproteins. They do not stop the DNA copy from entering the host chromosome.
w.CCR5 antagonists: Maraviroc acts at the very first step by occupying the CCR5 coreceptor. It blocks entry and cannot stop insertion in cells the virus has already entered.

pt.say: Step 4, Integration, shows integrase inserting the DNA as a permanent provirus, and the integrase inhibitors, the -tegravir drugs, sit on that step.

q: Protease inhibitors prevent HIV from producing infectious virions by blocking cleavage of which precursor?
x: The viral protease cuts the gag-pol polyprotein into mature capsid proteins and the enzymes reverse transcriptase, integrase and protease itself. Protease inhibitors, the -navir drugs, therefore leave virions that bud but stay immature and noninfectious.

w.The gp120 envelope protein: gp120 is the finished surface protein that binds CD4. The viral protease acts on the gag-pol polyprotein, not on gp120.
w.Newly made viral RNA: Viral RNA is copied from the provirus by host RNA polymerase and is not cut by any protease. Protease inhibitors act on proteins after translation.
w.The integrated provirus: The provirus is DNA fixed in the host chromosome. Neither the viral protease nor protease inhibitors act on it, which is why therapy cannot clear this reservoir.
w.The host CD4 receptor: CD4 is a human cell-surface protein that gp120 binds. The viral protease acts only on viral polyproteins, so the receptor is unaffected.

pt.say: Step 6 shows the protease cutting polyproteins into a mature p24 capsid, with protease inhibitors, the -navir drugs, blocking it; the polyprotein is the one made at step 5, gag-pol.

q: Which antiretroviral class binds reverse transcriptase at an allosteric site and needs no intracellular activation?
x: NNRTIs such as efavirenz and nevirapine bind a pocket on reverse transcriptase away from the active site and lock the enzyme in an inactive shape. They already work as given, so they need no phosphorylation, unlike NRTIs, which host kinases activate and which act as chain terminators.

w.Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibit: NRTIs bind the active site after host kinases turn them into triphosphates, and then end the growing chain. They are prodrugs that need activation.
w.Integrase strand transfer inhibitors: Integrase inhibitors block strand transfer by the integrase enzyme. They target a different enzyme and act after reverse transcription is complete.
w.Protease inhibitors: Protease inhibitors block the viral protease at the budding stage. They act on proteins, not on reverse transcription.
w.Fusion inhibitors: Enfuvirtide binds gp41 outside the cell to stop envelope fusion, a very early step. It is an injected peptide and never reaches reverse transcriptase.

pt.say: Step 3, Reverse transcription, lists NNRTIs with the allosteric site label, so the class that binds reverse transcriptase away from the active site and needs no activation is the NNRTIs.

q: In what form does HIV persist in resting CD4 cells and cause rebound when therapy stops?
o: Free virions in lymph node fluid
Viral RNA free in the cytoplasm
x: Integrase inserts the DNA copy of the genome into the host chromosome, and a resting memory CD4 cell can carry that integrated provirus silently for years without making virus. Antiretrovirals act on replicating virus and cannot remove it, so viral load rebounds when therapy stops.

w.Episomal circular DNA: Circular episomes are how herpes simplex virus and HPV persist, in neurons and basal keratinocytes. HIV, a retrovirus, is spliced permanently into a host chromosome.
w.Free virions in lymph node fluid: Free virions are cleared within days and fall to undetectable levels on therapy. They reflect ongoing replication, not the silent reservoir that outlives treatment.
w.Viral RNA free in the cytoplasm: Viral RNA in the cytoplasm is made from the provirus when a cell is activated. It is degraded or packaged into virions within hours and is not a stable reservoir.
w.Antibody-coated virions: Antibody-coated virions are cleared by phagocytes. They are not the source of persistent infection and cannot restart replication without an infected cell.

pt.say: Step 4 shows integrase inserting the DNA as a permanent provirus; a resting CD4 cell can carry that integrated provirus silently and restart virus production when therapy stops.

q: Fourth-generation HIV assays detect antibodies plus which viral capsid antigen that appears before seroconversion?
x: p24 is the capsid protein of HIV and is released into the blood in large amounts early in infection, before antibodies form. Fourth-generation assays detect HIV antibodies together with p24 antigen, which shortens the window period compared with antibody-only tests.

w.gp120: gp120 is the envelope protein that binds CD4. Antibodies against envelope proteins are what antibody tests detect, so it is not the early antigen.
w.gp41: gp41, the transmembrane envelope protein, is an early target of antibody. It is the target of antibody, not the free antigen detected before seroconversion.
w.p17: p17 is the matrix protein beneath the envelope. It is not an antigen used in clinical assays, so detecting it would not shorten the window period.
w.Reverse transcriptase: Reverse transcriptase is an enzyme packaged inside virions, and its level in blood is much lower than p24. The assays target p24 and HIV RNA instead.

pt.say: The step 6 label shows protease cutting polyproteins into a mature p24 capsid, the capsid antigen that appears in blood early and that fourth-generation assays detect.

q: At what point in prenatal care should every pregnant patient first be offered HIV screening?
o: Only after reporting a risk behavior
At the first prenatal visit, opt-out
At 28 weeks with the glucose challenge
At 36 weeks with group B strep culture
x: Every pregnant patient is offered opt-out HIV screening at the first prenatal visit, with a fourth-generation antigen/antibody test. Starting treatment early cuts the risk of passing HIV to the baby to a very low level.

w.Only after reporting a risk behavior: Risk-based screening misses many infections, because patients may not disclose or recognize exposure. Guidelines screen everyone with an opt-out approach.
w.At 28 weeks with the glucose challenge: By 28 weeks much of the chance to suppress the virus before delivery is lost. The glucose challenge is a gestational diabetes screen, not an HIV test.
w.At 36 weeks with group B strep culture: The 36-week culture guides group B strep prophylaxis. Testing for HIV that late leaves too little time to suppress the virus before delivery.
w.After the 20-week anatomy scan: The anatomy scan looks for structural defects and is unrelated to infection screening. Waiting until 20 weeks delays antiretroviral treatment that should start as early as possible.

hl: First visit: blood type, HIV, HBsAg, syphilis, urine culture
pt.say: The first-visit row of the prenatal timeline lists blood type, HIV, HBsAg, syphilis and urine culture, so HIV screening is offered at the first prenatal visit.

q: Which test of lesion fluid is the most sensitive for diagnosing genital herpes and typing the virus?
x: PCR of lesion swab fluid detects herpes simplex DNA with the highest sensitivity and tells HSV-1 from HSV-2. A Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells but is insensitive and cannot separate herpes simplex from varicella-zoster.

w.Tzanck smear: A Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells, which both herpes simplex and varicella-zoster cause. It cannot name the virus or its type, and it misses many cases.
w.Viral culture: Culture can type the virus, but it is less sensitive than PCR and takes days. It has largely been replaced by nucleic acid testing.
w.HSV IgG serology: Type-specific IgG blood tests can be negative early in a first infection and show only past exposure. They do not reliably diagnose a current ulcer.
w.Direct fluorescent antibody stain: Direct fluorescent antibody staining of lesion cells is fast but misses many infections. It is much less sensitive than amplifying viral DNA.

pt.say: In the herpes row of the genital ulcer table, the clue column lists Tzanck smear and lesion PCR; PCR is the more sensitive test and also tells HSV-2 from HSV-1.

q: Which antiviral is started at 36 weeks of pregnancy to suppress recurrent genital herpes before delivery?
x: Acyclovir or valacyclovir is started at 36 weeks in women with a history of genital herpes. Suppression cuts recurrences and viral shedding, so lesions at delivery are less likely and cesarean delivery for active lesions is needed less often.

w.Foscarnet: Foscarnet is reserved for acyclovir-resistant herpes, usually in AIDS. It is given intravenously and is toxic to the kidneys, so it is not used for routine suppression.
w.Ganciclovir: Ganciclovir treats cytomegalovirus disease and causes neutropenia. It is not the standard drug for herpes simplex suppression.
w.Ribavirin: Ribavirin is highly teratogenic and not used in pregnancy. It treats RSV and hepatitis C, not herpes simplex.
w.Cidofovir: Cidofovir is given intravenously with probenecid and saline for resistant or cytomegalovirus infection because it harms the kidneys. It is far too toxic for routine suppression.

hl: Acyclovir from 36 weeks if herpes history
pt.say: Under prevent at delivery in the birth-canal panel, the label reads acyclovir from 36 weeks if herpes history, so acyclovir or valacyclovir suppression starts at 36 weeks.

q: A woman in labor has active genital herpes lesions or prodromal symptoms. Which delivery is recommended?
o: Vaginal delivery with acyclovir for the newborn afterward
x: Active lesions or prodromal symptoms at the start of labor mean virus is shedding in the birth canal, so cesarean delivery lowers the risk of neonatal herpes, a severe infection of the skin, eyes and mouth, brain or whole body. Women with a history but no lesions or prodrome can deliver vaginally.

w.Vaginal delivery after intravenous acycl: Acyclovir given to the mother does not stop shedding at delivery, so it cannot replace cesarean delivery when lesions are present.
w.Vacuum-assisted vaginal delivery: Vacuum or forceps delivery injures the baby's scalp and exposes it to infected secretions. It adds risk and does not replace cesarean.
w.Vaginal delivery with acyclovir for the: Giving the newborn acyclovir afterward does not replace avoiding exposure in the birth canal. When lesions are present, cesarean delivery lowers the risk.
w.Induction with early amniotomy: Early rupture of membranes and induction prolong the baby's exposure to infected genital secretions, so this plan adds risk.

hl: Cesarean for HSV lesions or prodrome
pt.say: The prevent-at-delivery list says cesarean for HSV lesions or prodrome, because the fetus meets the virus in the birth canal during vaginal birth.

q: Which statement correctly describes valacyclovir?
o: Cytosine nucleotide analog given with probenecid
x: Valacyclovir is the valine ester of acyclovir. Esterases in the gut and liver remove the valine, giving much higher acyclovir blood levels than oral acyclovir. The active drug and its activation by viral thymidine kinase are unchanged.

w.Valine ester prodrug of ganciclovir: That describes valganciclovir, the oral prodrug of ganciclovir used for cytomegalovirus. The names differ by one syllable, but it targets CMV, not herpes simplex.
w.Pyrophosphate analog needing no activati: Foscarnet is the pyrophosphate analog. It binds viral DNA polymerase directly with no kinase activation, is given intravenously and is reserved for resistant virus.
w.Cytosine nucleotide analog given with pr: Cidofovir is the cytosine nucleotide analog that bypasses viral kinases. It needs probenecid and saline to protect the kidneys and is given intravenously for resistant virus.
w.Prodrug of penciclovir: Famciclovir is the prodrug converted to penciclovir. It is a separate guanosine analog that also needs viral thymidine kinase.

pt.say: The top box of the acyclovir diagram labels valacyclovir as the oral prodrug, with esterases removing valine to release acyclovir.

q: Which action of acyclovir triphosphate inhibits herpes simplex replication?
o: Direct binding to the polymerase pyrophosphate site
Blocking virion release by neuraminidase inhibition
Chain termination after competing with guanosine
Preventing uncoating through the M2 channel
x: Acyclovir triphosphate competes with deoxyguanosine triphosphate for viral DNA polymerase. Once built into the chain, it ends the chain because it has no 3' hydroxyl for the next nucleotide. Uninfected cells lack the viral thymidine kinase that makes the first phosphate, so they are spared.

w.Direct binding to the polymerase pyropho: Binding the pyrophosphate site is how foscarnet works, with no activation needed. Acyclovir must first be turned into a triphosphate that mimics guanosine.
w.Blocking virion release by neuraminidase: Neuraminidase inhibitors such as oseltamivir block release of influenza virions. Herpes viruses have no neuraminidase.
w.Blocking cleavage of viral polyproteins: Blocking polyprotein cleavage describes HIV protease inhibitors. Herpes simplex copies its DNA with its own polymerase, which is acyclovir's target.
w.Preventing uncoating through the M2 chan: Amantadine blocks the influenza M2 channel to prevent uncoating. Herpes viruses use a different route, and acyclovir acts later, at DNA synthesis.

pt.say: The lower boxes show the viral DNA chain stops growing with no 3' hydroxyl, chain termination, after viral DNA polymerase inserts acyclovir triphosphate, which competes with guanosine.

q: Why does acyclovir shorten a herpes outbreak but not cure the infection?
o: Latent virus has no active thymidine kinase or polymerase to act on
Latent virus is integrated into host DNA like HIV provirus
Antibodies neutralize the drug in the ganglia
Resistance develops in all patients within weeks
x: Acyclovir works only where viral DNA is being copied, because it needs viral thymidine kinase to activate it and then blocks viral DNA polymerase. Latent herpes is a quiet episome in sacral neurons that makes almost no viral protein, so there is nothing to activate the drug. Reactivation restarts from that untouched reservoir when therapy stops.

w.Acyclovir cannot enter neurons: IV acyclovir treats herpes encephalitis, so it does reach nervous tissue. The drug is simply inactive without the viral kinase.
w.Latent virus is integrated into host DNA: Herpes simplex stays as a circular episome in the neuron nucleus and does not integrate, which is HIV's strategy. Either way, a silent genome lacks the machinery that antiviral drugs need.
w.Antibodies neutralize the drug in the ga: Antibodies bind virions and viral proteins, not small-molecule drugs, so they cannot inactivate acyclovir.
w.Resistance develops in all patients with: Resistance from thymidine kinase mutations is uncommon in healthy people and appears mainly in AIDS. It cannot explain why relapse follows stopping therapy in every patient.

pt.say: In the box on why healthy cells are spared, activation happens only where the virus is replicating, so latent virus with no active replication has nothing to activate the drug.

q: Which HPV types cause most genital warts?
x: Low-risk HPV types 6 and 11 cause genital warts, the soft cauliflower-like condylomata acuminata, and they stay as episomes without integrating. They rarely cause cancer, unlike types 16 and 18, which integrate and use E6 and E7 to drive cervical and anal cancers.

w.Types 16 and 18: These are the high-risk types that cause most cervical, anal and oropharyngeal cancers. Their E6 and E7 proteins target p53 and Rb after integration, while warts come from low-risk types.
w.Types 31 and 33: Types 31 and 33 are high-risk types covered by the 9-valent vaccine and can cause high-grade cervical lesions. They are not the wart types.
w.Types 1 and 2: Types 1 and 2 cause common warts of the hands and plantar warts on the soles. They are skin warts, not genital lesions.
w.Types 6 and 18: This pair mixes a wart type with a cancer type. Type 18 is high risk, and the two wart types are 6 and 11.

pt.say: In the low-risk branch of the diagram, types 6 and 11 stay episomal and cause warts, unlike types 16 and 18 on the high-risk side that integrate.

q: Which HPV proteins inactivate p53 and Rb, respectively, in high-risk HPV infection?
x: High-risk HPV integrates into the host genome, and E6 and E7 surge. E6 binds p53 and tags it for degradation, so damaged cells neither stop in G1 nor die. E7 binds Rb and releases E2F, pushing the cell into S phase. L1 and L2 are the capsid proteins.

w.E7 and E6: The order is reversed. E7 inactivates Rb and releases E2F, and E6 degrades p53.
w.L1 and L2: L1 and L2 are the capsid proteins that self-assemble into the virus-like particles in the vaccine. They play no role in disabling tumor suppressors.
w.E1 and E2: E1 and E2 are early proteins that help copy viral DNA. They do not disable tumor suppressors directly.
w.E4 and E5: E4 helps release virions from the upper epithelium, and E5 boosts growth factor receptor signaling. Neither is the main protein that disables p53 or Rb.

pt.say: Under E6, the diagram shows binds p53 and tags it for decay, and under E7 it shows binds Rb and releases E2F, so E6 and E7 inactivate p53 and Rb in that order.

q: At what age is routine HPV vaccination recommended to begin?
o: After the first abnormal Pap test
x: Routine HPV vaccination starts at age 11 to 12, before most people are exposed. The vaccine prevents new infection and does not treat existing disease, so it works best before exposure.

w.Age 16 to 17: Waiting until the late teens leaves many teenagers exposed before they are protected. Routine vaccination starts earlier.
w.Age 21: Age 21 is when cervical cytology screening begins. The vaccine is meant to be given long before that, before exposure.
w.Age 30: Age 30 is when HPV testing joins cervical screening. By then most people have already been exposed to HPV.
w.After the first abnormal Pap test: The vaccine prevents new infection and does not treat existing disease or an abnormal Pap test. It is given before exposure, not after a lesion appears.

pt.say: In the vaccine box, the label starts with age 11 to 12, so routine HPV vaccination begins at age 11 to 12, before exposure.

q: In people with HIV, which screening is added to cervical screening because of the higher HPV-related cancer risk?
x: HIV weakens T-cell control of HPV, so infections persist and lesions progress faster. Anal cytology is added to cervical screening in people with HIV, because anal cancer, also caused by high-risk HPV, is far more common in this group.

w.Annual mammography: Mammography is not tied to HIV or HPV. Breast screening follows the general age-based schedule.
w.Serum CA-125: Screening for ovarian cancer with CA-125 is not recommended, because it is neither sensitive nor specific. HIV does not change that, and ovarian cancer is not caused by HPV.
w.Low-dose chest CT: Low-dose CT is for older adults with a heavy smoking history. HIV alone does not trigger it, and HPV does not cause lung cancer.
w.Endometrial biopsy: Endometrial biopsy is for abnormal bleeding or high-risk situations such as Lynch syndrome, not for routine screening. Estrogen exposure, not HPV, drives endometrial cancer.

pt.say: In the HIV or immunosuppressed box, the labels read start at diagnosis, screen more often, lifelong, and add anal cytology to the cervical screening.

q: Which drugs make up daily oral pre-exposure prophylaxis against HIV?
x: Daily oral PrEP is tenofovir with emtricitabine, two NRTIs that keep drug in the tissues HIV first infects. Long-acting injectable cabotegravir is another option. PrEP requires a negative HIV test first.

w.Zidovudine with lamivudine: This is an older treatment backbone for established infection, not prophylaxis. Zidovudine causes bone marrow suppression and macrocytic anemia.
w.Efavirenz with abacavir: Abacavir needs HLA-B*57:01 testing, and efavirenz causes vivid dreams and other CNS effects. Neither is used for prophylaxis.
w.Lopinavir with ritonavir: This boosted protease inhibitor pair treats established HIV and has many drug interactions. It is not a prophylaxis regimen.
w.Raltegravir with maraviroc: An integrase inhibitor with a CCR5 antagonist is a salvage-type treatment combination. Maraviroc needs a tropism test, and this pair is not used to prevent infection.

q: Why is low-dose ritonavir added to many protease inhibitor regimens?
o: It induces CYP3A4, lowering partner drug toxicity
It adds a second antiviral action at integrase
It blocks CCR5 to prevent viral entry
It prevents lipodystrophy from the protease inhibitor
It inhibits CYP3A4, raising levels of the partner drug
x: Ritonavir is itself a protease inhibitor, but it is given at doses too low to suppress HIV. Its purpose is to inhibit CYP3A4, the liver enzyme that clears most protease inhibitors, so a small dose raises the level and prolongs the half-life of the partner drug. The price is many drug interactions.

w.It induces CYP3A4, lowering partner drug: Enzyme induction is what rifampin and phenytoin do, and it lowers drug levels. Ritonavir does the opposite: it inhibits the enzyme, so it raises levels and raises the risk of interactions.
w.It adds a second antiviral action at int: Integrase inhibitors are separate drugs ending in -tegravir. At boosting doses ritonavir has no meaningful antiviral effect and works only through drug metabolism.
w.It blocks CCR5 to prevent viral entry: CCR5 blockade is the job of maraviroc, which acts at entry. Ritonavir acts on liver enzymes and the viral protease, not on the coreceptor.
w.It prevents lipodystrophy from the prote: Protease inhibitors cause lipodystrophy, hyperglycemia and high lipids, and ritonavir adds to these effects. Its role is to raise drug levels, not to protect.
